title: Launch pads flood with water so a rocket’s own noise doesn’t damage it

cover.alt: Looking down from a launch tower into a flame trench where torrents of white water spray out in all directions.

body: A rocket’s exhaust leaves faster than sound, and the shockwaves and roar bouncing back off the pad approach **200 dB**, enough to damage the rocket, its payload and its crew. A payload can safely take only about 145 dB. So just before ignition the pad releases a deluge of water into the path of the exhaust. On the Space Shuttle’s pads it cut the noise to about 142 dB, and the huge white clouds at liftoff were mostly steam from water the exhaust boiled away, not smoke.

slides.alt: Three views of a water test at a launch pad: water sprays out beneath the launch tower into the flame trench, then a drone looks straight down on torrents of white water pouring around the tower’s base.
slides.caption: October 2023: pad 39B in Florida tests its water system under the launch tower for NASA’s Artemis II rocket, flooding the area where the engines will fire.
slides.credit: NASA/Cory S Huston · Public domain · excerpt

slides.heading: Water held ready for one launch
slides.note: Pad 39B can pour out up to 1.1 million US gallons (4.2 million litres) a minute

slides.label: heat-shield tiles lost or damaged on the first Shuttle launch
slides.text: In 1981 the pressure wave from its ignition contributed to the loss of 16 tiles and damage to 148 more. The water system at both pads was then modified.

slides.question: At a Space Shuttle launch, what were the huge white clouds mostly made of?
slides.explanation: The rocket exhaust boiled away huge quantities of the sound-suppression water, making clouds of wet steam.
